name: Drafting Sustainability Disclosures
title: Drafting Sustainability Disclosures
answer: This page covers the use of AI to draft sustainability disclosures, including greenhouse gas emissions reports, climate risk narratives, and governance statements. It addresses how systems assemble quantitative data and qualitative text for frameworks such as the CSRD, ISSB standards, and TCFD recommendations. The focus is on drafting, summarization, consistency checking, and mapping content to disclosure requirements. It is written for accountants and sustainability professionals who prepare or review corporate reports.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers the use of AI to draft sustainability disclosures, including greenhouse gas emissions reports, climate risk narratives, and governance statements. It addresses how systems assemble quantitative data and qualitative text for frameworks such as the CSRD, ISSB standards, and TCFD recommendations. The focus is on drafting, summarization, consistency checking, and mapping content to disclosure requirements. It is written for accountants and sustainability professionals who prepare or review corporate reports.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These tools typically run on cloud document platforms connected to internal data sources such as ERP systems, utility invoices, supplier surveys, and prior year reports. Large language models are often paired with retrieval systems that pull from a company's own emissions records and policy documents. The infrastructure may include data pipelines that convert activity data, such as kilowatt hours or litres of fuel, into carbon dioxide equivalent figures before drafting. Access controls and versioned document stores are common because multiple teams contribute to a single disclosure.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually begins by extracting structured data from spreadsheets, invoices, and facility records, then applying emission factors to calculate totals by scope. The AI drafts narrative sections that explain methodology, year over year changes, and targets, while cross checking figures against the quantitative tables. It can also compare draft text against the specific wording and data points required by a reporting framework and flag missing or inconsistent items. A human reviewer edits the output, confirms the calculations, and approves the final text before filing or publication.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are inaccurate emission factors, hallucinated citations, and greenwashing through overly positive language that is not supported by data. Because disclosures can be filed with regulators or shared with investors, companies need a clear audit trail showing which source document or calculation produced each figure. Human sign-off remains essential, and many teams keep a log of prompts, retrieved passages, and model versions. This page describes common practice and does not provide legal advice on liability for filed disclosures.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more automated assurance, where AI checks a draft against source data and flags unsupported claims before a human auditor reviews it. Real time disclosure may become more common as carbon accounting ledgers update continuously rather than once a year. Regulatory tagging, such as machine readable sustainability data, is likely to push these tools toward structured output that can be validated by software. Over time, drafting may shift from generating prose to assembling auditable, data linked statements that update as underlying figures change.
